deficiencies.description: The structured transcript completely omits the geographical variations in cancer incidence, specifically that liver and nasopharyngeal carcinomas are prevalent in Chinese populations, and that liver cancer has a large infectious component.

source.evidence: liver cancer and nasopharyngeal carcinomas are very big in Chinese populations. There's also a large infectious element to liver cancer.
source.location: Towards the end of the transcript, in the discussion about the incidence of various tumours.

deficiencies.suggestedFix: Add a bullet point under a relevant section (e.g., 'Comparative Oncology and Tumour Incidence') noting geographical differences, specifically the prevalence of liver and nasopharyngeal cancers in Chinese populations and the infectious link to liver cancer.
deficiencies.outputLocation: Section: Comparative Oncology and Tumour Incidence or Morbidity and Mortality in Cancer

deficiencies.description: The structured version states cervical screening led to a substantial decline in mortality, but omits the crucial clinical caveats that this decline is mostly seen in older women, and that current deaths are primarily among those who decline screening or are not followed up.

source.evidence: This hasn't changed much for the younger populations, but the, if you like, the women that are still dying of cervical cancer would be the ones that either are not followed up after their screen or that have declined screening altogether.
source.location: In the section discussing the success of cervical cancer screening.

deficiencies.suggestedFix: Expand the cervical screening section to clarify that the mortality decline is prominent in older populations, and remaining deaths are largely due to non-participation or lack of follow-up.

deficiencies.description: The description of cervical dysplasia mentions mitotic figures extending throughout the layers, but omits the normal baseline (mitosis strictly at the basal layer, cells flattening with tiny nuclei towards the surface). This strips the dysplasia mechanism of its necessary histological contrast.

source.evidence: these squames are flattened, the nuclei are tiny, and you only ever get mitotic cells here at this basement layer... contrast that with what you'll see in a dysplastic situation... mitotic cells that are occurring throughout the thickness
source.location: In the discussion of the Pap smear and normal versus abnormal cervical histology.

deficiencies.suggestedFix: Include a brief description of the normal squamous epithelium (mitosis confined to the basal layer, cells flattening apically with small nuclei) to properly contrast with the dysplastic state.

deficiencies.description: The transcript notes a specific demographic detail for malignant mesenchymal tumours (sarcomas), stating they typically occur in adolescence and young adulthood. This detail is missing.

source.evidence: malignant tumors, for example, originating from mesenchymal lineage cell types, they're extremely rare... They usually occur in young adulthood, in adolescence and young adulthood.
source.location: In the discussion regarding the incidence of benign versus malignant tumours.

deficiencies.suggestedFix: Add the typical age of onset (adolescence and young adulthood) to the description of malignant mesenchymal tumours.
deficiencies.outputLocation: Section: Tumour Nomenclature and Classification or a new Incidence subsection

deficiencies.description: The structured version omits the clinical/histopathological concept of checking for 'clear margins' around a biopsy to confirm the entire tumour has been removed.

source.evidence: You'll also hear about looking for clear margins around any kind of biopsy, to see that you have lifted out the entire tumor.
source.location: In the section defining invasion and describing biopsy limitations.

deficiencies.suggestedFix: Mention the clinical practice of histopathologists checking for 'clear margins' to ensure complete excision.

considered.whyNotRaised: The structured version uses the clinical term 'pancytopenia', which was not explicitly spoken by the lecturer. However, it is a perfectly accurate medical synthesis of the described marrow interference causing broad cytological deficits (anaemia and infection), so it is an acceptable summarization rather than an unsourced addition.
